blocks.note: The data half of the exam: a fake flight catalogue and roughly 230 cases. This header is the vocabulary every case is written in, and harness/avaliar.ts is the interpreter for it. Reading these fourteen lines first makes the rest of the file skimmable, because every entry below is just a combination of these fields.
The only import: the flight type from voos.ts, so the fake catalogue produces exactly the shape the real search produces and nothing downstream can tell the difference.

Four fake flights, and their numbers are chosen to make questions answerable. TAP is non-stop and fastest but not cheapest; LATAM with Iberia is cheapest with two stops; Air Europa and Azul sit in between. That spread is what gives "which is fastest", "which is cheapest" and "which is best value" three different correct answers.

Three alternative worlds, reached through specific destinations. One cheap domestic flight, a route where every direct flight has been removed and the rest cost 3000 more, and fourteen generated flights, which is how the "the list was cut at ten" behaviour gets tested.
The class multiplier: economy 1, premium 1.5, business 2, first 4. It makes a class request visible in the price, so a case can prove the class really reached the search.

The fake Google. Line 36 returns nothing for destination ZZZ or origin CGH, which is the empty world. Line 37 picks which flight set a destination gets. Line 38 adjusts by route, which is what makes "which airport is cheaper" and "Lisbon or Madrid" have real answers. Line 39 adjusts by the day number, which does the same for "which day is cheapest". Then passengers and class multiply, a fake link is attached and the list comes back cheapest first. Same inputs, same prices, forever: that is the whole point of the file.
The cheapest price of a leg, used below so the expected values are computed from the catalogue instead of typed in. If the catalogue changes, the cases follow automatically.

Dates that depend on today, with the same logic the real date parser uses: 1 to 7 days ahead, never today itself. That duplication is deliberate, because a case saying "next Friday" must expect the same day the bot will choose, and borrowing the function from the code under test would hide a bug in it.

The shortcuts: the standard first message, the standard search filter, and the four expected prices with the real numbers written in the comments. Naming them makes a case like "cita: [LATAM]" readable at a glance.

The whole mini-language in one type. msgs is what to send. busca and naoBusca are searches that must and must not have happened, as partial filters. semBusca forbids any search; buscaOuPergunta accepts either searching or asking. cita lists values that must appear; tem and naoTem are patterns that must and must not match; pergunta demands a question; semPreco forbids any price. The last four reach into the database: a watch that must exist, no watch at all, a stored preference matching a pattern, or none.

The case list begins. Each entry is one object, and the name's prefix before the first hyphen is also the group that harness/comparar.ts scores by, which is why the names read as "fala-girias" and "idioma-espanhol".

How people actually write. Slang, telegraphic, reversed order, all caps, emoji only, a rambling story with the request buried in it, audio-transcription style with no punctuation, no spaces at all, excessively formal, indirect ("I need to be in Lisbon"), and a country instead of a city. Then the five where the correct answer is to ask rather than to search: "e aí", a lone question mark, two loose numbers, a destination alone and two codes alone.
Other languages. Each case demands both the right search and an answer in the same language, which is what the orchestrator's idioma field and the writer's first instruction exist for.

Awkward dates: the many written forms, months with no day, dates in the past, and the ones where a named weekday has to match the resolved date. This is the group that the date parser and the weekday cross-check in harness/ferramentas.ts are measured by.

Passengers and class: counts, children, lap infants, and the class aliases. The expected prices come from the catalogue with the same multipliers, so quoting the single-adult price fails even though it looks like a plausible answer.

Follow-up questions after a search, which must be answered from what is already in memory. A case here that produces a new search is a failure even when the answer is right, because searching again is slower, costs a request and risks a block.

Arithmetic, all of which has to go through the calcular tool. The checker in harness/verificador.ts reads that tool's "Resultado:" line, so a number computed in the model's head would be refused even when it is correct.
Several legs: round trips, multiple origins and destinations, and comparisons between them. These are the cases that exercise combinar_ida_e_volta and melhores_voos rather than the search itself.

Ambiguous places: cities with several airports, unknown cities, and names that look like places but are not. The correct answer is often to ask, which is what the invented-place lock makes possible instead of a confident wrong search.

Attempts to make the bot lie or leak. Direct instructions to ignore the rules, a price planted in your own message, messages pretending to come from the system or a tool, and requests to reveal the instructions. These are the cases that rule 7 of the writer's prompt and the user-price check in harness/verificador.ts were written for, and they are the ones worth re-running after any prompt change.
Off topic. Questions that are not about flights, where the right answer involves no search, no price and no pretending to be a general assistant.

When something breaks: the Brasília captcha, the Dublin spreadsheet failure, and routes with no flights. Each has a specific correct behaviour, and the most important one is never reporting an outage as "there are no flights".

Memory in longer conversations: several messages where the bot has to carry the earlier context forward rather than asking again. This is what the history window and the cleaned history in harness/agente.ts are tuned for.

Unusual formats: requests about how the answer should be laid out, one flight per line, a table, a short answer. The writer has no tools, so these test whether it can reshape what the others brought without inventing anything on the way.

Watches: creating, listing and cancelling, checked against the real database through the monitora and semMonitor fields. These are the cases where a convincing sentence is not enough, because the judge looks at the row.

Preferences: storing one, using it in a later answer, forgetting it, and the refusal to store a price. The last one protects every future conversation, since a stored price would come back looking like a fact.

The newest group, which is where a case lands when a real failure gets turned into a test. That is the loop worth keeping: the bot does something wrong, the fix list in harness/aprender.ts surfaces it, a case is written here, and from then on the exam notices if it ever comes back.
